lesson.title: Two Plots, One Story: Assembling the Complete Bode Plot
lesson.summary: A full Bode plot stacks the magnitude and phase plots on a shared logarithmic frequency axis, giving a complete, verifiable picture of a filter's behavior from a handful of landmark numbers.
lesson.body:
Bode Magnitude Plot and Bode Phase Plot each tell half of a circuit's story on their own, one tracking how much a signal's amplitude is scaled at each frequency, the other tracking how much it is delayed in phase. A Bode Plot in the complete sense is simply the two of them stacked together, sharing the same horizontal, logarithmic frequency axis, so an engineer can read both amplitude and timing behavior for the same frequency in one glance.

Assemble the complete picture for the RC low pass filter used throughout this chapter, R = 1000 ohms, C = 1 microfarad, corner frequency wc = 1/RC = 1000 rad/s, or fc = 159.155 Hz. In the top, magnitude panel, the plot is flat at roughly 0 dB out to about w = 100 rad/s, then bends downward, passing through -3.010 dB exactly at w = 1000 rad/s, and continuing to fall at -20 dB per decade, reaching -20.043 dB at w = 10000 rad/s and -40.000 dB at w = 100000 rad/s, all of these values verified by direct calculation earlier in this chapter.

In the bottom, phase panel, directly below the magnitude panel and sharing the same frequency axis, the plot is flat near 0 degrees out to w = 100 rad/s, where it reads -5.711 degrees, then slopes down through -45.000 degrees exactly at the shared corner frequency w = 1000 rad/s, continuing to -84.289 degrees at w = 10000 rad/s and approaching -90 degrees as frequency climbs further. Because both panels share the same vertical gridline at w = 1000 rad/s, a reader can look straight down from the -3 dB point in the magnitude panel to find the -45 degree point in the phase panel directly beneath it, confirming both landmarks describe the exact same corner frequency.

This side by side layout is exactly why Bode plots are the standard way to document a filter or amplifier's frequency behavior in datasheets and lab reports. A single glance tells you the passband gain, the corner frequency, the roll off rate, and the phase margin available for feedback design, four separate pieces of information that would otherwise require four separate calculations. The straight line asymptotes covered separately for magnitude and phase let a designer sketch this entire two panel picture from memory, needing only the location of the corner frequency and the fixed corrections at that one point, -3 dB in magnitude and -45 degrees in phase.

For circuits with multiple poles or zeros, the same construction still applies, each pole or zero contributes its own corner frequency, its own -20 dB per decade slope change, and its own 45 degree per decade phase contribution, and because decibels and phase angles both add when stages are cascaded, the individual straight line contributions from every pole and zero simply sum together to build the composite Bode plot for the whole circuit, no matter how many stages the full system eventually contains.
